```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(survival)
```

# 0. Data

The `veteran` data in the `survival` package (Kalbfleisch & Prentice, 1980).
Treatment and prior therapy are recoded as labelled factors so the output
and plots are easier to read.

```{r data}
data(veteran, package = "survival")
vet <- veteran
vet$trt   <- factor(vet$trt,   levels = c(1, 2),  labels = c("Standard", "Test"))
vet$prior <- factor(vet$prior, levels = c(0, 10), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
str(vet)
```

Check the counts quoted in the report (137 patients, 69/68 per arm,
128 deaths, 9 censored):

```{r counts}
nrow(vet)
table(vet$trt)
table(Status = vet$status)      # 1 = died, 0 = censored
table(vet$trt, vet$celltype)    # patients per treatment x cell type group
table(vet$trt, vet$status)      # deaths/censored per arm
summary(vet[, c("time", "karno", "diagtime", "age")])
```

**Interpretation.**

* The counts match the trial description: 137 patients (69 standard,
  68 test), 128 deaths and 9 censored times.
* Censoring is balanced between the arms (5 standard, 4 test), so it does
  not favour either treatment. This supports the independent-censoring
  assumption.
* Cell type is unbalanced between the arms despite randomization: the
  standard arm has more small-cell patients (30 vs 18) and the test arm has
  twice as many adeno patients (18 vs 9). Both are poor-prognosis types, so
  an unadjusted treatment comparison is partly a cell-type comparison. This
  is the reason for the stratified log-rank test (4.2) and for adjusting for
  cell type in the AFT model (4.4).
* Treatment x cell-type groups contain between 9 (standard, adeno) and 30
  (standard, small cell) patients, so the interaction test (4.5) has
  limited power.
* Survival time is strongly right-skewed: median 80 days, mean 121.6,
  maximum 999.
* Karnofsky score covers almost the whole scale (10-99, median 60), and age
  runs from 34 to 81.
* Time since diagnosis is very skewed (median 5 months, maximum 87), so a
  few patients could have a large influence on its coefficient.

# 4.0 Expected distribution

**Why:** before estimating anything, we use what we know about the data to
propose candidate distributions for T. T is time to death in men with
advanced, inoperable lung cancer, so we expect short, strongly right-skewed
survival times (confirmed above: median 80 days, mean 121.6, max 999).

* *Exponential* (constant hazard): the simplest model, used by Prentice (1973).
* *Weibull* (hazard only rising or only falling).
* *Log-logistic / lognormal* (hazard rises then falls): common in cancer
  survival, especially in a mixed population like this one.

Only 7% of times are censored, so a histogram of observed times gives a fair
rough picture of the shape.

```{r expected-dist}
hist(vet$time, breaks = 30, main = "Observed survival times",
     xlab = "Days since randomization")
```

**Interpretation.**

* Most deaths occur in the first 200 days, with a long thin tail out to
  999 days. The shape is consistent with all four candidates.
* The histogram cannot tell them apart. That needs the nonparametric
  estimates of S(t) and H(t), which the plots in 4.3 use.

# 4.1 Kaplan-Meier estimates

**Why:** the Kaplan-Meier estimator estimates S(t) without assuming a
distribution and handles right censoring. Variances use Greenwood's formula
(the `survfit` default). We use log-log confidence intervals, which stay
inside [0, 1].

```{r km-fit}
km_all  <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,        data = vet, conf.type = "log-log")
km_trt  <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ trt,      data = vet, conf.type = "log-log")
km_cell <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = vet, conf.type = "log-log")
```

Median survival times with 95% CIs:

```{r km-medians}
print(km_all)
print(km_trt)
print(km_cell)
```

Estimated survival at 3, 6 and 12 months by treatment:

```{r km-times}
summary(km_trt, times = c(90, 180, 365))
```

```{r km-plot-overall}
plot(km_all, xlab = "Days since randomization", ylab = "Estimated S(t)",
     main = "Kaplan-Meier estimate, all patients (95% log-log CI)")
```

```{r km-plot-trt}
plot(km_trt, col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Days since randomization", ylab = "Estimated S(t)",
     main = "Kaplan-Meier estimate by treatment")
legend("topright", legend = levels(vet$trt), col = c("blue", "red"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

```{r km-plot-cell}
plot(km_cell, col = 1:4, lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Days since randomization", ylab = "Estimated S(t)",
     main = "Kaplan-Meier estimate by cell type")
legend("topright", legend = levels(vet$celltype), col = 1:4,
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

**Interpretation: all patients.**

* Median survival is 80 days (95% CI 52-100). About half the patients die
  within 3 months, and very few survive past a year.
* The tail beyond 365 days rests on 4-6 patients per arm, so estimates there
  are imprecise.

**Interpretation: by treatment.**

| | Median (95% CI) | S(90) | S(180) | S(365) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard | 103 (54-126) | 0.55 | 0.21 | 0.07 |
| Test | 52.5 (43-90) | 0.38 | 0.23 | 0.11 |

* There is no sign that the test treatment prolongs survival. Its median is
  lower, but the confidence intervals overlap heavily.
* The curves cross at about 150-200 days: standard does better early, and
  test does slightly better later.
  * When curves cross, the log-rank test loses power because early and late
    differences cancel out. We therefore also run the Peto-Peto version
    (`rho = 1`) in 4.2.
  * The crossing also suggests the treatment effect may not be constant.
* Part of the early gap may come from cell type: the test arm had twice as
  many adeno patients, and adeno patients die fastest. The stratified test
  (4.2) and the AFT model (4.4) adjust for this.

**Interpretation: by cell type.**

| | Median (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Large | 156 (100-216) |
| Squamous | 118 (44-242) |
| Small cell | 51 (24-61) |
| Adeno | 51 (24-90) |

* The cell types fall into two groups.
  * Small cell and adeno patients die quickly; every adeno patient had died
    by about 180 days.
  * Large cell and squamous patients survive about 2-3 times longer.
* The large-cell and squamous curves cross. Large cell does better in the
  first ~150 days and squamous does better later, with the longest tail.
  * The curves differ in shape, not only in location.
  * This matters when we choose a distribution (4.3) and check whether one
    scale parameter fits all groups.

# 4.2 Log-rank tests

**Why:** the log-rank test compares whole survival curves
(H0: S1(t) = S2(t) for all t) without assuming a distribution, and is the
standard test for a randomized trial. It is most powerful when one curve stays
above the other. The treatment curves cross at about 150-200 days, so we also
run the `rho = 1` version (Peto-Peto), which puts more weight on early
differences, as a check.

Treatment (H0: S_test = S_standard):

```{r lr-trt}
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ trt, data = vet)
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ trt, data = vet, rho = 1)
```

Cell type (H0: all four curves equal, df = 3):

```{r lr-cell}
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = vet)
```

Treatment, stratified by cell type. **Why:** cell type is unbalanced between
the arms (e.g. 9 vs 18 adeno patients), so this compares treatments within
each cell type and then combines the results.

```{r lr-trt-strat}
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + strata(celltype), data = vet)
```

**Interpretation.**

| Test | Chi-square | df | p-value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treatment, log-rank | 0.01 | 1 | 0.93 |
| Treatment, Peto-Peto (`rho = 1`) | 0.87 | 1 | 0.35 |
| Cell type, log-rank | 25.4 | 3 | 0.00001 |
| Treatment, stratified by cell type | 0.70 | 1 | 0.40 |

* **Treatment:** no evidence of a difference between the two
  chemotherapies (p = 0.93).
  * Observed deaths almost equal expected deaths in both arms (64 vs 64.5
    standard, 64 vs 63.5 test).
  * The Peto-Peto test, which weights early deaths more, is also not
    significant (p = 0.35). So the conclusion does not depend on the curves
    crossing.
  * We do not reject H0: S_test(t) = S_standard(t). The data give no
    evidence that the test chemotherapy prolongs survival.
* **Cell type:** survival differs strongly between the four cell types
  (p = 0.00001).
  * Small cell (45 observed vs 30.1 expected deaths) and adeno (26 vs 15.7)
    have more deaths than expected.
  * Squamous (31 vs 47.7) and large cell (26 vs 34.5) have fewer.
  * This confirms the two groups seen in the Kaplan-Meier curves. Cell type
    is an important prognostic factor and must be included in the
    regression model.
* **Treatment adjusted for cell type:** still no difference (p = 0.40).
  * Within cell types, the test arm has slightly more deaths than expected
    (64 vs 59.8), but not significantly.
  * The cell-type imbalance between the arms does not explain the lack of
    a treatment effect.

# 4.3 Choosing a distribution

**Why:** an AFT model needs a distribution for T. We check the candidates
from 4.0 graphically, then by likelihood.

* **Graphical check:** the Nelson-Aalen estimate of the cumulative hazard
  H(t) is transformed so that each candidate distribution would give a
  straight line:
  * exponential: H(t) against t (a straight line through the origin)
  * Weibull: log H(t) against log t
  * log-logistic: log[(1 - S)/S] = log(exp(H) - 1) against log t
  * lognormal: qnorm(1 - S) against log t
* **Nelson-Aalen estimate:** we get it as in the course notes, from the
  Fleming-Harrington fit (`type = "fh2"`), with H(t) = -log S(t).

```{r na-fit}
na_all <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = vet, type = "fh2")
na_df  <- data.frame(t = na_all$time, S = na_all$surv)
na_df  <- subset(na_df, S > 0 & S < 1)      # drop points where transforms are undefined
na_df$H    <- -log(na_df$S)
na_df$logt <- log(na_df$t)
```

```{r linearizing-plots, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(na_df$t, na_df$H, type = "s", xlab = "t (days)", ylab = "H(t)",
     main = "Exponential: H(t) vs t")
plot(na_df$logt, log(na_df$H), type = "s", xlab = "log t", ylab = "log H(t)",
     main = "Weibull: log H(t) vs log t")
plot(na_df$logt, log(exp(na_df$H) - 1), type = "s", xlab = "log t",
     ylab = "log[(1-S)/S]", main = "Log-logistic: log-odds vs log t")
plot(na_df$logt, qnorm(1 - na_df$S), type = "s", xlab = "log t",
     ylab = "qnorm(1-S)", main = "Lognormal: qnorm(1-S) vs log t")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Weibull plot by cell type.** If one AFT model with a common scale fits,
these four lines should be roughly parallel (shifted only).

```{r weibull-by-cell}
na_cell <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = vet, type = "fh2")
cols <- 1:4
plot(NULL, xlim = range(log(vet$time)), ylim = c(-5, 2),
     xlab = "log t", ylab = "log H(t)", main = "Weibull plot by cell type")
for (i in seq_along(levels(vet$celltype))) {
  s  <- na_cell[i]
  ok <- s$surv > 0 & s$surv < 1
  lines(log(s$time[ok]), log(-log(s$surv[ok])), type = "s", col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
}
legend("bottomright", legend = levels(vet$celltype), col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

**Likelihood comparison.** We fit each distribution with `survreg`, twice:

* **Without covariates:** describes the distribution of T for the whole
  sample.
* **With all covariates:** this is what the AFT model will actually use,
  because the distribution is assumed for the error term after adjusting
  for covariates.

The Weibull, log-logistic and lognormal models have the same number of
parameters, so the one with the largest log-likelihood fits best. Exponential
is Weibull with scale = 1, so we compare those two with a likelihood ratio
test (df = 1).

```{r dist-fits}
dists <- c("exponential", "weibull", "loglogistic", "lognormal")

fit0 <- lapply(dists, function(d) survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = vet, dist = d))
fitX <- lapply(dists, function(d) survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + celltype + karno +
                                            diagtime + age + prior, data = vet, dist = d))

dist_table <- data.frame(
  distribution        = dists,
  loglik_no_covariates = sapply(fit0, function(f) f$loglik[2]),
  loglik_covariates    = sapply(fitX, function(f) f$loglik[2]),
  scale_covariates     = sapply(fitX, function(f) f$scale)
)
dist_table
```

Likelihood ratio test, exponential vs Weibull (H0: scale = 1):

```{r lrt-exp-weibull}
lrt <- function(small, big, df) {
  stat <- 2 * (big$loglik[2] - small$loglik[2])
  c(LR = stat, df = df, p = pchisq(stat, df, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
lrt(fit0[[1]], fit0[[2]], 1)   # no covariates
lrt(fitX[[1]], fitX[[2]], 1)   # all covariates
```


**Interpretation: linearizing plots.**

* All four plots are roughly straight through the middle of the data, so
  the graphs alone do not clearly separate the candidates. This is common
  with skewed data and few late survivors.
* Exponential (H(t) vs t) fits least well. The plot is close to linear for
  the first ~400 days, then flattens and jumps where only a few patients
  remain at risk.
* Weibull, log-logistic and lognormal all look reasonably linear against
  log t. The likelihood comparison is needed to choose between them.

**Interpretation: Weibull plot by cell type.**

* Small cell and adeno lie above squamous and large cell, which confirms
  their higher cumulative hazard.
* The lines are roughly parallel through the middle, which supports a
  common-scale AFT model.
* The squamous line is flatter at the top and crosses large cell at about
  log t = 5.5 (around 250 days). The squamous group may have a different
  shape, so we check a cell-type-specific scale in 4.6.

**Interpretation: likelihood comparison.**

| Distribution | Log-lik, no covariates | Log-lik, all covariates | Scale (covariates) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exponential | -751.2 | -716.2 | 1 (fixed) |
| Weibull | -748.1 | -715.6 | 0.93 |
| Log-logistic | -750.3 | **-711.9** | 0.58 |
| Lognormal | -749.5 | -714.6 | 1.06 |

* **Without covariates**, Weibull fits best, and the exponential is
  rejected (LR = 6.26, df = 1, p = 0.012).
* **With covariates**, the exponential is no longer rejected against the
  Weibull (LR = 1.22, df = 1, p = 0.27; Weibull scale 0.93, close to 1).
  * This agrees with Prentice (1973), who found the Weibull shape close
    to 1.
  * The two results differ because, without covariates, T mixes patients
    with very different prognoses. A mix of high-risk patients (who die
    early) and low-risk patients makes the overall hazard appear to fall
    over time. Once covariates account for these differences, a constant
    hazard is adequate within the Weibull family.
* **With covariates, log-logistic fits best.** Its log-likelihood is 3.6
  higher than the Weibull's, with the same number of parameters.
  * The two models are not nested, so they cannot be compared with a
    likelihood ratio test. With equal numbers of parameters, the larger
    log-likelihood is the better fit (this is also what AIC would give).
  * The log-logistic scale is 0.58 < 1, which means a hazard that rises
    and then falls. This matches the expectation in 4.0 for advanced
    cancer.
* **Decision:** we use the **log-logistic AFT model** as the main model.
  We also fit the **Weibull** model (which includes Prentice's exponential
  as a special case) for comparison. Section 4.6 checks this choice with
  Cox-Snell residuals.

# 4.4 Accelerated failure time regression

**Model:** log T = x'beta + sigma W, where W has a standard logistic
distribution (log-logistic T).

* exp(beta_j) is a **time ratio**: the factor by which survival time is
  multiplied for a one-unit increase in x_j, holding the other covariates
  fixed. A time ratio above 1 means longer survival.
* We start with all covariates. We remove non-significant ones using Wald
  tests for single coefficients and likelihood ratio tests for groups (cell
  type has 3 coefficients).
* Treatment stays in the model whatever its p-value, because it answers
  the primary question.

```{r aft-full}
aft_full <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + celltype + karno + diagtime +
                      age + prior, data = vet, dist = "loglogistic")
summary(aft_full)
```

Likelihood ratio tests for dropping each covariate from the full model:

```{r aft-drop}
drop_lrt <- function(term, df) {
  smaller <- update(aft_full, as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", term)))
  lrt(smaller, aft_full, df)
}
rbind(
  celltype = drop_lrt("celltype", 3),
  karno    = drop_lrt("karno", 1),
  diagtime = drop_lrt("diagtime", 1),
  age      = drop_lrt("age", 1),
  prior    = drop_lrt("prior", 1),
  trt      = drop_lrt("trt", 1)
)
```

Reduced model with the non-significant covariates (diagtime, age, prior)
removed together, and a joint test that they can be dropped (df = 3):

```{r aft-reduced}
aft_red <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + celltype + karno,
                   data = vet, dist = "loglogistic")
summary(aft_red)
lrt(aft_red, aft_full, 3)
```

Time ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals for the reduced model:

```{r time-ratios}
time_ratios <- function(fit) {
  est <- coef(fit)
  se  <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[names(est)]
  round(cbind(TR    = exp(est),
              lower = exp(est - 1.96 * se),
              upper = exp(est + 1.96 * se)), 3)
}
time_ratios(aft_red)
```

The same reduced model under the Weibull distribution, for comparison:

```{r aft-weibull}
aft_red_w <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + celltype + karno,
                     data = vet, dist = "weibull")
summary(aft_red_w)
time_ratios(aft_red_w)
```

**Interpretation: model selection.**

| Term dropped from full model | LR | df | p |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cell type | 15.33 | 3 | 0.0016 |
| Karnofsky score | 52.91 | 1 | < 0.0001 |
| Time since diagnosis | 0.04 | 1 | 0.84 |
| Age | 0.92 | 1 | 0.34 |
| Prior therapy | 0.23 | 1 | 0.63 |
| Treatment | 0.24 | 1 | 0.62 |

* Only Karnofsky score and cell type are significant.
* Time since diagnosis, age and prior therapy can be dropped together
  (LR = 1.21, df = 3, p = 0.75).
* The **final model** is therefore log T = trt + celltype + karno. Treatment
  stays in because it is the primary question.
* This agrees with Prentice (1973), who found performance status to be the
  main prognostic factor. We also keep cell type, which is clearly
  significant here.

**Interpretation: time ratios (log-logistic, final model).**

| Covariate | Time ratio (95% CI) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Test vs standard | 0.95 (0.67-1.34) | No evidence of a treatment effect (p = 0.76) |
| Small cell vs squamous | 0.50 (0.31-0.80) | Survival about half as long |
| Adeno vs squamous | 0.46 (0.27-0.78) | Survival about half as long |
| Large vs squamous | 0.97 (0.58-1.62) | No difference |
| Karnofsky, +1 point | 1.037 (1.028-1.046) | |
| Karnofsky, +10 points | 1.43 (1.31-1.56) | Survival about 43% longer |

* **Treatment:** after adjusting for cell type and Karnofsky score, the
  test chemotherapy multiplies survival time by an estimated 0.95. The CI
  runs from a 33% reduction to a 34% increase, so the data are consistent
  with no effect. This answers the primary objective: there is no evidence
  that the test chemotherapy prolongs survival.
* **Karnofsky score** is the strongest predictor. Each 10-point increase
  multiplies survival time by about 1.43.
* **Cell type:** small cell and adeno patients survive about half as long
  as squamous patients with the same treatment and Karnofsky score. Large
  cell and squamous do not differ. This matches the two groups in the
  Kaplan-Meier curves.
* **Predicted medians:** for a log-logistic model the median of T is
  exp(x'beta), because the standard logistic distribution has median 0.
  * Squamous, standard treatment, Karnofsky 60: exp(2.519 + 0.0359 x 60)
    = about 107 days.
  * The same patient with small cell: about 53 days.
  * Squamous, standard treatment, Karnofsky 30: about 37 days.
* **Weibull comparison:** the conclusions are the same. Treatment is not
  significant (TR 0.81, p = 0.25), Karnofsky is strong (1.34 per 10
  points), and small cell and adeno are worse. One difference is large
  cell vs squamous: TR 0.68 under Weibull vs 0.97 under log-logistic,
  not significant in either. This reflects the crossing large-cell and
  squamous curves, which the two distributions handle differently.
  Log-logistic fits better (log-likelihood -712.5 vs -715.9), so we keep it
  as the main model.

# 4.5 Treatment x cell-type interaction

**Why:** Prentice (1973) found that the treatment effect seemed to point in
different directions for different cell types but did not test it. We add
the treatment x cell-type interaction to the final model and test the three
interaction terms together (H0: no interaction) with a likelihood ratio test,
df = 3, under both log-logistic and Weibull.

```{r interaction-lrt}
aft_int   <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ trt * celltype + karno,
                     data = vet, dist = "loglogistic")
aft_int_w <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ trt * celltype + karno,
                     data = vet, dist = "weibull")
summary(aft_int)
lrt(aft_red,   aft_int,   3)   # log-logistic
lrt(aft_red_w, aft_int_w, 3)   # Weibull
```

Treatment time ratio within each cell type. **Why:** this is the same model
written so that each coefficient is directly the treatment effect for one
cell type, which is easier to read than interaction terms.

```{r interaction-by-cell}
aft_nest <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype + celltype:trt + karno,
                    data = vet, dist = "loglogistic")
time_ratios(aft_nest)[grep("trt", names(coef(aft_nest))), ]
```

**Interpretation.**

| Distribution | LR | df | p |
|---|---|---|---|
| Log-logistic | 0.78 | 3 | 0.85 |
| Weibull | 6.98 | 3 | 0.07 |

| Cell type | Treatment time ratio, test vs standard (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Squamous | 1.09 (0.51-2.32) |
| Small cell | 0.90 (0.50-1.62) |
| Adeno | 1.14 (0.54-2.43) |
| Large | 0.75 (0.37-1.55) |

* **No significant interaction.** Under the log-logistic model there is
  no evidence that the treatment effect depends on cell type (p = 0.85).
  Under the Weibull model the evidence is weak and not significant at the
  5% level (p = 0.07). The Weibull model fits worse (4.3, 4.4), so we rely
  on the log-logistic result.
* **The pattern Prentice described is visible but small.** The estimated
  treatment effect points in different directions: slightly longer
  survival on the test treatment for squamous and adeno, slightly shorter
  for small cell and large cell.
  * These are the same directions as Prentice's (1973) adjusted expected
    survival times, where the test treatment was higher for squamous and
    adeno and lower for small and large cell.
  * Every confidence interval contains 1, and the joint test shows these
    differences are consistent with chance.
* **This answers Prentice's open question:** the apparent differences in
  treatment effect across cell types are not statistically significant.
* **Caveat:** the groups are small (9-30 patients each), so the test has
  low power. A non-significant result does not show the effects are equal;
  the confidence intervals are wide enough to allow moderate differences.

# 4.6 Model assessment

**Why:** the conclusions depend on the log-logistic AFT model being
adequate. We check it in three ways:

1. **Cox-Snell residuals.**
   * r_i = -log S(t_i | x_i) from the fitted model. If the model is right,
     the r_i behave like a censored sample from the unit exponential
     distribution.
   * So the Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard of the r_i should follow the
     45-degree line.
   * We compute them for both the log-logistic and Weibull final models
     to compare the two distributions.
     * Log-logistic: r = log(1 + exp(z)).
     * Weibull: r = exp(z).
     * In both, z = (log t - x'beta) / sigma.
2. **Deviance residuals** plotted against the linear predictor and against
   time. They should show no pattern.
3. **Common scale across cell types.**
   * The Weibull plot in 4.3 suggested squamous may have a different
     shape.
   * We let each cell type have its own scale (`strata(celltype)`, as in
     the course notes) and test this against a common scale with a
     likelihood ratio test (df = 3).

```{r cox-snell}
cs_resid <- function(fit, dist) {
  z <- (log(vet$time) - fit$linear.predictors) / fit$scale
  if (dist == "loglogistic") log(1 + exp(z)) else exp(z)
}
cs_ll <- cs_resid(aft_red,   "loglogistic")
cs_w  <- cs_resid(aft_red_w, "weibull")

cs_plot <- function(r, title) {
  f <- survfit(Surv(r, vet$status) ~ 1, type = "fh2")
  plot(f$time, -log(f$surv), type = "s", xlab = "Cox-Snell residual",
       ylab = "Estimated cumulative hazard", main = title)
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
cs_plot(cs_ll, "Log-logistic")
cs_plot(cs_w,  "Weibull")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r deviance}
dev_ll <- residuals(aft_red, type = "deviance")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(aft_red$linear.predictors, dev_ll, xlab = "Linear predictor",
     ylab = "Deviance residual", main = "vs linear predictor")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
plot(vet$time, dev_ll, log = "x", xlab = "Time (days, log scale)",
     ylab = "Deviance residual", main = "vs time")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# patients with large residuals
vet[abs(dev_ll) > 2.5, c("time", "status", "trt", "celltype", "karno")]
```

```{r scale-by-cell}
aft_strat <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + celltype + karno + strata(celltype),
                     data = vet, dist = "loglogistic")
aft_strat$scale
lrt(aft_red, aft_strat, 3)
```

**Interpretation: Cox-Snell residuals.**

* **Log-logistic:** the cumulative hazard of the residuals follows the
  45-degree line closely up to about 3.5. Beyond that, a few large
  residuals sit near the line, but there are too few points in the tail to
  judge.
* **Weibull:** the plot falls below the line from about 2.5 onward and
  ends far to the right (largest residual about 8). The Weibull model
  underestimates the hazard for the longest survivors.
* This confirms the choice in 4.3: the **log-logistic model fits
  better**.

**Interpretation: deviance residuals.**

* **Against the linear predictor:** a random scatter around 0 with no
  trend or funnel shape. The covariates enter the model in an adequate
  form.
* **Against time:** a rising trend. This is expected by construction and
  does not indicate lack of fit. For patients with similar covariates, the
  one who dies earlier always has a more negative residual, so plotting a
  residual against its own response must slope upward.
* **Large residuals (|r| > 2.5):** four of 137 patients.
  * Three squamous patients died much earlier than predicted. Two died on
    day 1 (Karnofsky 20 and 50) and one on day 11 (Karnofsky 70).
  * One small-cell patient with Karnofsky 40 lived 392 days, much longer
    than predicted.
  * These look like real outcomes rather than data errors, so we keep
    them.
  * Squamous patients appear among both the earliest deaths and the
    longest survivors, which fits the scale result below.

**Interpretation: common scale across cell types.**

| Cell type | Squamous | Small cell | Adeno | Large |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Scale | 0.79 | 0.61 | 0.45 | 0.41 |

* A common scale is **rejected** (LR = 11.56, df = 3, p = 0.009).
* The spread of log survival time differs by cell type. Squamous is the
  most variable, with both very early deaths and the longest survivors.
  Large cell and adeno are the least variable.
* This matches the crossing large-cell and squamous Kaplan-Meier curves
  (4.1) and the flatter squamous line in the Weibull plot (4.3).
* So the common-scale model in 4.4 is a simplification. We check below
  whether the main conclusions change when each cell type has its own
  scale.

## 4.6.1 Sensitivity analysis: cell-type-specific scale

**Why:** the common-scale assumption was rejected, so we refit the final
model and the interaction test with a separate scale for each cell type. If
the treatment and Karnofsky conclusions are unchanged, they do not depend
on that assumption.

```{r sens-strat}
summary(aft_strat)
time_ratios(aft_strat)
```

Interaction test with cell-type-specific scales (df = 3):

```{r sens-interaction}
aft_int_strat <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ trt * celltype + karno + strata(celltype),
                         data = vet, dist = "loglogistic")
lrt(aft_strat, aft_int_strat, 3)
```

Cox-Snell residuals for the stratified model:

```{r sens-cox-snell}
sc_i <- aft_strat$scale[as.character(vet$celltype)]
z_s  <- (log(vet$time) - aft_strat$linear.predictors) / sc_i
cs_s <- log(1 + exp(z_s))
cs_plot(cs_s, "Log-logistic, cell-type-specific scale")
```

**Interpretation.**

| | Common scale (4.4) | Cell-type-specific scale |
|---|---|---|
| Test vs standard, TR (95% CI) | 0.95 (0.67-1.34) | 0.92 (0.67-1.27) |
| Small cell vs squamous | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| Adeno vs squamous | 0.46 | 0.47 |
| Large vs squamous | 0.97 | 0.96 |
| Karnofsky, +1 point | 1.037 | 1.037 |
| Interaction test p-value | 0.85 | 0.83 |
| Log-likelihood | -712.5 | -706.8 |

* **The conclusions do not change.**
  * Treatment is still not significant (p = 0.62).
  * The Karnofsky and cell-type time ratios are almost identical.
  * There is still no treatment x cell-type interaction (p = 0.83).
* The stratified model fits better (log-likelihood 5.7 higher, p = 0.009
  from 4.6). Its Cox-Snell residuals follow the 45-degree line closely up
  to about 4, slightly better than the common-scale model.
* **Conclusion:** we report the common-scale model (4.4) as the main model
  because it is simpler and matches the analysis plan. Allowing each cell
  type its own scale improves the fit but leaves every conclusion
  unchanged, so the results do not depend on the common-scale assumption.

# 4.8 Supplementary group comparisons

**Why:** these plots show the group differences behind the model
results. They are descriptive and can be moved into Sections 4.1-4.2 of
the report.

**Treatment within each cell type.** This shows the interaction question
directly. The within-cell log-rank p-values are descriptive only: the groups
are small and four tests are made, so they are not a substitute for the
formal interaction test in 4.5.

```{r km-trt-by-cell, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (ct in levels(vet$celltype)) {
  d  <- subset(vet, celltype == ct)
  km <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ trt, data = d)
  lr <- survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ trt, data = d)
  p  <- pchisq(lr$chisq, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
  plot(km, col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2, xlab = "Days", ylab = "S(t)",
       main = sprintf("%s (log-rank p = %.2f)", ct, p))
  legend("topright", legend = levels(vet$trt), col = c("blue", "red"),
         lwd = 2, bty = "n")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Karnofsky score groups.** We use the categories described by Prentice
(1973): 10-30 completely hospitalized, 40-60 partially confined to hospital,
70-90 able to care for self. This makes the strongest covariate effect
visible.

```{r km-karno}
vet$karno_grp <- cut(vet$karno, breaks = c(0, 30, 60, 100),
                     labels = c("10-30 hospitalized", "40-60 partial", "70+ self-care"))
table(vet$karno_grp)
km_karno <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ karno_grp, data = vet, conf.type = "log-log")
print(km_karno)
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ karno_grp, data = vet)
plot(km_karno, col = 1:3, lwd = 2, xlab = "Days since randomization",
     ylab = "Estimated S(t)", main = "Kaplan-Meier estimate by Karnofsky group")
legend("topright", legend = levels(vet$karno_grp), col = 1:3, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

**Interpretation: treatment within each cell type.**

| Cell type | Log-rank p | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Squamous | 0.12 | Test does better after about 150 days |
| Small cell | 0.13 | Standard does better; no test patient survives past about 100 days |
| Adeno | 0.63 | Curves close together |
| Large | 0.29 | Standard does better in the first ~200 days |

* None of the within-cell differences is significant. The directions
  match Prentice (1973) and our time ratios in 4.5: test is favoured for
  squamous, standard for small cell and large cell.
* These four tests are descriptive. The formal answer is the interaction
  test in 4.5 (p = 0.85).

**Interpretation: Karnofsky groups.**

| Karnofsky group | n | Median survival (95% CI) |
|---|---|---|
| 10-30, completely hospitalized | 22 | 19.5 days (13-25) |
| 40-60, partially confined | 57 | 52 days (30-80) |
| 70+, able to care for self | 58 | 132 days (110-162) |

* Survival differs strongly between the groups (log-rank chi-square = 51,
  df = 2, p < 0.0001).
* All 22 completely hospitalized patients died, all within about 150 days.
  There were 22 deaths against 6.5 expected.
* Median survival rises from about 3 weeks to about 4 months across the
  three groups. This is the clearest picture of why Karnofsky score is the
  strongest predictor in the AFT model and in Prentice (1973).
